chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Durays al-Kunasi from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
The divine limits (hudud) are not pardoned except by the Imam. As for what is the right of the people, there is no harm in pardoning it without the Imam.

key_terms.الْإِمَام: The Imam, referring to the divinely appointed leader with authority
key_terms.الْحُدُود: Divine limits or fixed punishments prescribed by God
key_terms.حَقِّ النَّاس: The rights of people, referring to personal claims or debts

ai.seo_question: Who has the authority to pardon divine limits (hudud) versus the rights of people in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith clarifies the jurisdictional boundary between *hudud* (fixed divine penalties) and *huquq al-nas* (rights of people), asserting that while the Imam holds exclusive authority to pardon divine limits, private individuals may forgive their own rights without his direct intervention. This distinction underscores the Imam’s role as the ultimate executor of divine law, while preserving the autonomy of individuals in civil matters. The ruling reflects the broader Shia principle that *hudud* are matters of public interest (*maslaha*) requiring centralized authority, whereas *huquq al-nas* are primarily private claims.
